items: First-line pharmacologic management of GERD is PPIs.

blocks.text: Antacids (PRN) • Maalox, Mylanta, Rolaids, Tums • Increases pH for 20–30 minutes
• Fastest relief
H2 receptor • Cimetidine (Tagamet) • Decreases acid production for 6–12 hours

items: antagonists • Famotidine (Pepcid) • Provides relief in 60 minutes
Proton pump • Omeprazole (Prilosec) • Reduces gastric acid secretion

blocks.text: inhibitors (PPI) • Lansoprazole (Prevacid) • Provides relief in 1 to 3 days
If there is no symptom relief of GERD after 8 weeks on a PPI—REFER!
The 41-year-old female responds well to esomeprazole. Her GERD symptoms have resolved during 8 weeks of therapy. What should be done next?
items: Remove the diagnosis of GERD from the patient’s chart.
Refer the patient for an endoscopy to confirm GERD.
Discontinue the medication and see if symptoms persist after 2 to 4 weeks.

blocks.text: A 62-year-old non-Hispanic white male with a history of smoking presents to the clinic. He has been taking an OTC PPI for heartburn for 5 years and reports worsening pyrosis and regurgitation. Which of the following is the biggest concern?
items: The patient could have bone loss from prolonged PPI use.
The patient could have Barrett’s esophagus or esophageal cancer.
The patient may be taking his PPI incorrectly.
The patient could be experiencing angina.
